about: Editable element manifest: every element each template draws (at the example content), in storybit_composition_schema.json format. Element ids are what props.elements / props.groups target. Boxes are canvas px at the settled frame for the example props — they change with content, so the editor should re-read positions from the live render.

template.description: Quoting a line from a court judgment, report, contract, law or policy: "the document actually says…".
Showing how people, companies, places or events are connected in a scam, crime or scandal.
Introducing a case, a suspect, an accused company or an investigation in true-crime / scam stories.
Showing a historical photograph: "This is Bombay in 1947…".
Listing clues, ideas, facts we know, or open questions in a loose, investigative way.
Explaining how something works step by step: a workflow, a procedure, a pipeline, a supply chain with a value at each stage.
One thing leads to another: cause → effect, problem → solution, trigger → response, or a short chain of three.
Explaining a choice or eligibility step by step: "If X, then… otherwise…".
Something narrows stage by stage: applicants → selected, visitors → buyers, users → paying users.
Who reports to whom, a family tree, a group of companies, a classification (up to 4 levels).
How a system works inside: what connects to what (UPI, a data centre, an app, the power grid).
Weighing the good and the bad of one thing: a policy, a product, a decision.
Two rivals head to head — phones, companies, players, cities, policies — on a few measures.
Debunking a common belief: "Many people think X. In fact, Y."
Values compared across 3–10 categories: states, companies, years, products; rankings with numbers; a threshold to beat.
A trend over time: growth, a crash, a peak, a recovery, or 2–4 things changing over the same years.
"X% of…", market share, a budget split, or how a whole divides into 2–6 parts.
One value on a scale with good / bad zones: AQI, inflation vs target, a score, how full something is.
A top-N ranking: richest, biggest, most populous, most-watched — with or without values.
"1 in 5…", "3 out of 10…", "40% of…": a share of people or things that should be felt, not just read.
Pointing at something inside the footage: circle a face, underline a line in a document, cross out a claim.
Opening the video or a new section; narration introduces a named topic.
Introducing an event, place, person or organisation together with 2–4 key facts (date, place, category, source).
Narration states one striking figure: "₹4,200 crore", "73% of Indians", "3 million users".
Two figures are compared, or the same metric before and after: "from ₹12 lakh to ₹45 lakh", "India 7% vs China 5%".
Narration quotes a real person, speech, document or report word for word.
A thesis, warning, takeaway or "here's the thing" moment the viewer must remember.
"3 reasons why", "the causes are", features, examples, steps without order, or a recap of key points.
Comparing 2–3 options, products, plans or countries on the same attributes (a comparison table).
Explaining what is on screen while the footage keeps playing: key facts about a place, product or event.
A single word the narrator hits hard: "BANNED", "FREE", "GONE", "NEVER".
A punchy statement in 2–4 beats, often building up: "Not ₹10 lakh. Not ₹1 crore. ₹100 crore."
Opening a loop with a question the video will answer: "But why did it fail?", "Who really owns it?"
Burned-in captions that follow the voiceover word by word (Shorts, Reels, hook sections).
Introducing where a story happens: fly from the globe into a place — or show several places / countries at once.
Showing how far something reaches from a place: missile range, delivery radius, flight range, impact zone.
A journey or trade route across places: a trip, a smuggling route, a supply chain, a historic voyage.
A new chapter or part of a long video begins.
Each item of a "Top N" countdown or listicle starts: "Number 7…".
Early in the video (30–60 s) and at most once more: ask viewers to subscribe.
The final 5–20 seconds of every video, under YouTube end-screen elements.
The closing line of the video: "Thank you for watching", with a friendly emoji animation.
The first time an important person is named: who they are, in one card.
Introducing a person with the key facts about them: a founder, politician, athlete, accused.
Several dated events in order: a history, a biography, a company's journey, how something unfolded.
Phases or projects over time: a roadmap, a construction schedule, overlapping eras, "what happens when".
Quoting a real post from X / Twitter, Threads or similar: who said it, what, when, how it spread.
Retelling a conversation, a scam message thread, or a story told through chat.
Narration cites a news report or several headlines about the same story.
Historical or archival news: "In 1991 the papers reported…". Real, sourced reports only.
"Everyone was searching for…", "I typed X into the search bar": a query being typed with suggestions.
A phone alert moment: a bank debit SMS, an app ping, a news alert, an OTP message.
Showing a specific photo that needs a name or one line of explanation (a place, an object, an archive picture).
"Many examples": several pictures at once, a collage.
A quick sequence of pictures, or photos in chronological order (a city through the decades, prices over the years).
Then vs now, before vs after: the same place, product or person compared in two pictures.
An establishing shot of a place: name the city, landmark or region on screen.
A person speaks or appears on screen: put their name and role at the bottom.
A figure is mentioned while the footage should keep playing.
Pointing out specific things in the footage or a photo: "this is the control room", "note the crack here".
Whenever a number, quote or claim on screen comes from a source — attach it for credibility.
